question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The Harsk Valley and the Teluan Coast each have a centuries-old tradition of casting bronze bells for temples.
• In both traditions, a bell is considered finished only when it rings a single pure pitch, chosen to match the chant of the temple where it will hang.
• Harsk founders cast each bell a little thick and then reach the pitch by shaving metal from the inner wall with hand scrapers.
• Teluan founders never alter a bell after casting; they calculate the wall profile in advance and shape the clay mould to match it.
• In both traditions, a bell is sounded by a wooden beam hung from the temple frame beside the bell and swung against its rim.

The student wants to tell readers what the Harsk and Teluan founders have in common and then note where they part ways. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: In both the Harsk Valley and on the Teluan Coast, a bell counts as finished only when it rings one pure pitch, but Harsk founders shave the wall after casting while Teluan founders build the wall profile into the mould.
answer_b: Harsk founders cast each bell a little thick and then shave metal from the inner wall with hand scrapers, whereas Teluan founders never alter a bell after casting and instead shape the clay mould to a wall profile calculated in advance.
answer_c: Harsk and Teluan founders both cast bronze bells for temples, and in both traditions the bells are sounded by a wooden beam hung beside the bell and swung against its rim.
answer_d: Harsk and Teluan founders alike consider a bell finished only when it rings a single pure pitch, a pitch chosen to match the chant of the temple where the bell will hang.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because it accomplishes both parts of the student's goal in the right order. It first gives what the two traditions share: in both the Harsk Valley and on the Teluan Coast, a bell is finished only when it rings one pure pitch. It then gives a real divergence in how that pitch is reached: Harsk founders shave the wall after casting, while Teluan founders build the calculated wall profile into the mould and never alter the finished bell.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It accurately contrasts how Harsk founders (cast thick, then shave the inner wall) and Teluan founders (calculate the profile and shape the mould) tune their bells, but it never states what the two groups of founders share, so it covers only the second half of the goal.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It lists only what the two traditions share: both cast bronze bells for temples, and both sound their bells with a wooden beam hung beside the bell. It never states where the founders differ, so it covers only the first half of the goal.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It describes in detail what the two traditions share, namely that a bell is finished only when it rings a single pure pitch chosen to match the temple's chant, but it says nothing about where the traditions part ways, so it covers only the first half of the goal.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• A community land trust is a nonprofit organization that owns land and sells the houses on it to buyers, who then lease the land from the trust for a small annual fee.
• Marrow Creek's trust, founded in 1991, is the oldest of three trusts that were studied between 2014 and 2023.
• In Marrow Creek, 1.1% of the homes on trust land were foreclosed on, compared with 4.6% of comparable market-rate homes nearby.
• In Ostby, 0.8% of the homes on trust land were foreclosed on, compared with 3.9% of comparable market-rate homes nearby.
• In Telford Heights, 1.4% of the homes on trust land were foreclosed on, compared with 5.2% of comparable market-rate homes nearby.
• Only Telford Heights has a hardship loan fund, which paid out $212,000 to 37 trust homeowners during the study period.

The student wants to make a general claim about how community land trusts affect the financial stability of homeowners, one that the notes as a whole support. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: In Telford Heights, a hardship loan fund paid out $212,000 to 37 trust homeowners, and only 1.4% of the homes on trust land were foreclosed on.
answer_b: Community land trusts protect the financial stability of homeowners by pairing low-cost land leases with hardship loan funds.
answer_c: In all three communities studied, homes on trust-owned land were foreclosed on far less often than comparable market-rate homes nearby.
answer_d: Foreclosure affected 1.1% of trust homes in Marrow Creek and 0.8% in Ostby, versus 4.6% and 3.9% of nearby market-rate homes.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it makes a general claim that all three studied cases support. The notes report that in Marrow Creek (1.1% versus 4.6%), Ostby (0.8% versus 3.9%), and Telford Heights (1.4% versus 5.2%), homes on trust land were foreclosed on much less often than comparable market-rate homes nearby. Since foreclosure is a direct measure of whether homeowners keep their homes, this pattern across all three communities supports a broad statement about the stability that trust ownership gives homeowners, without relying on any detail that is true of only one place.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It describes only Telford Heights, using exact figures for the hardship fund and that city's foreclosure rate. It is a specific example from one case, not a general claim about community land trusts, and it does not draw on the results from Marrow Creek or Ostby.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. It makes a broad claim about community land trusts, but it credits their effect on homeowners to hardship loan funds, and the notes say only Telford Heights has one. Marrow Creek and Ostby had much lower foreclosure rates without such a fund, so the generalization rests on a feature found in only one of the three cases, not on the notes as a whole.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It places the foreclosure figures for two of the cities side by side, which is accurate, but it compares particular results and leaves out Telford Heights. It reports data for two cases rather than stating a general claim about community land trusts that all of the notes support.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1884, Ansel Lindqvist patented a steam-driven well pump.
• The Lindqvist pump moved water with a piston sliding inside a cylinder, as the older hand-lever pumps had done.
• The older lever pumps could lift water about 8 meters; the Lindqvist pump could lift it about 30 meters.
• Like the lever pumps, the Lindqvist pump was cast almost entirely from iron.
• Lever pumps needed a person at the handle for as long as water was wanted; the Lindqvist pump's steam engine worked without anyone pumping.
• Both kinds of pump were installed at farms and village wells across the region.
The student wants to point out something the newer pump could do that its predecessor could not. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Like the older lever pumps, the Lindqvist pump moved water with a piston in a cylinder and was cast almost entirely from iron.
answer_b: The Lindqvist pump could lift water about 30 meters, far higher than the 8 meters the older lever pumps could manage.
answer_c: The older lever pumps could lift water about 8 meters, but they needed a person at the handle for as long as water was wanted.
answer_d: Patented in 1884 by Ansel Lindqvist, the pump was installed, like the older lever pumps, at farms and village wells across the region.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. The goal is to point out something the newer pump could do that the older pumps could not. The notes state that the older lever pumps could lift water about 8 meters, while the Lindqvist pump could lift it about 30 meters. Because this choice contrasts the two lifting heights, it identifies a capability that only the newer pump had.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It describes the Lindqvist pump, but both features it names, moving water with a piston in a cylinder and being cast almost entirely from iron, are ones the notes say the older lever pumps shared. These features don't show anything the newer pump could do that its predecessor could not.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It accurately reports information from the notes, but every detail concerns the older lever pumps: their 8-meter lifting limit and their need for someone at the handle. It never says what the newer pump could do, so it doesn't accomplish the goal.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It mentions the Lindqvist pump, but the inventor's name and the 1884 patent date are not abilities, and the installation at farms and village wells is something the notes say both kinds of pump shared. It therefore doesn't identify something the newer pump could do that the older pumps could not.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 1993, Sesay selected the hardiest seedlings from the plants she had bred and replanted them over several seasons.
• Tumani-4 was released to farmers nationwide in 1999.
• Sesay began by collecting local rice varieties from floodplain villages in 1987.
• Trials in three districts in 1995 showed that the variety outyielded standard rice in dry seasons.
• Sesay, a plant breeder in Sierra Leone, developed Tumani-4, a rice variety suited to dry seasons.
• In 1991, she crossed the collected varieties with a high-yielding lab strain.

The student wants to trace how Sesay's work developed over time, from its starting point to the variety's arrival in farmers' fields. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: In 1993 Sesay selected hardy seedlings, and Tumani-4 was released nationwide in 1999; she then collected local rice varieties from floodplain villages in 1987, crossed them with a lab strain in 1991, and ran district trials in 1995.
answer_b: Sesay's work on Tumani-4 began with local rice varieties gathered from floodplain villages in 1987 and moved through a 1991 cross with a lab strain, district trials in 1993, and a 1995 seedling selection, ending with nationwide release in 1999.
answer_c: Released to farmers nationwide in 1999, Tumani-4 is a rice variety suited to dry seasons that Sesay, a plant breeder in Sierra Leone, developed from local floodplain rice varieties and a high-yielding lab strain.
answer_d: Sesay's work on Tumani-4 began with local rice varieties gathered from floodplain villages in 1987 and moved through a 1991 cross with a lab strain, a 1993 seedling selection, and 1995 district trials, ending with nationwide release in 1999.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer. The goal has two requirements: the events must be told in the order they actually happened, and the account must reach the point where the variety gets to farmers. The notes list the events out of order, so the dates have to be used to sort them: collecting local rice varieties (1987), crossing them with a lab strain (1991), selecting seedlings (1993), district trials (1995), and nationwide release (1999). Choice D presents exactly that order, with each step matched to its correct date, and ends with the 1999 release, so it shows how the work developed from its starting point to the variety's arrival in farmers' fields.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it gets the sequence wrong. It uses all of the events but does not follow the order of the dates (it opens with the 1993 selection and the 1999 release), and the word "then" turns that into a false sequence. It places the 1987 collection, the 1991 cross, and the 1995 trials after the 1999 release, when the dates show they came before it. The goal asks for how the work developed over time, and this choice misstates that development.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it misstates the order of two steps. It begins and ends at the right points (the 1987 collection and the 1999 release), but it places the district trials in 1993 and the seedling selection in 1995. The notes show the reverse: Sesay selected seedlings in 1993, and the district trials took place in 1995. Because the goal is to trace how the work developed over time, an account that swaps these steps misrepresents that development.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it does not trace a sequence. It states the 1999 release and gives background on what Tumani-4 is and what it was developed from, but it gives no dates or order for the steps in between. The goal asks how Sesay's work developed over time, and this choice only describes the outcome and its ingredients.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Environmental DNA (eDNA) is genetic material that animals shed into their surroundings, such as through skin cells and waste, and that can be collected from a water sample.
• In 2024, a team led by ecologist Marisol Ferreira-Okoye studied the Tarrin Creek watershed in the hills above Dellmoor.
• Searching streambeds by hand for the secretive Tarrin hellbender, a salamander, damages its habitat and still misses animals hiding under rocks.
• The team wanted to learn whether eDNA in stream water could show where hellbenders live without anyone having to turn over rocks.
• To test this, the team collected one-liter water samples at 16 stream sites, screened them for hellbender DNA, and also searched the same sites by hand.
• The water samples revealed hellbenders at 14 sites; the hand searches found them at 9.
The student wants to explain the researchers' reason for conducting the study to an audience unfamiliar with eDNA. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: Genetic material that animals shed into their surroundings can be collected from water, and in the Tarrin Creek study it revealed hellbenders at 14 of 16 sites, five more than hand searches did.
answer_b: Because searching by hand for a hidden stream salamander damages its habitat and still misses animals, the team tested whether traces of genetic material that animals leave in water could show where it lives.
answer_c: The researchers conducted the study because searching streambeds by hand for hellbenders damages habitat and misses hidden animals, so they tested whether eDNA could show where the salamanders live.
answer_d: The team collected one-liter water samples at 16 sites and screened them for hellbender DNA, genetic material that animals shed into their surroundings through skin cells and waste.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. The goal has two requirements: the sentence must give the researchers' reason for conducting the study (the aim, not the method or the result), and it must be understandable to readers who do not know what eDNA is. Choice B does both. It gives the reason (hand searches for the hellbender damage its habitat and still miss animals, so the team wanted another way to find out where the salamander lives) and it explains the unfamiliar term in plain words as "traces of genetic material that animals leave in water" instead of using the label "eDNA."
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. It explains what eDNA is in plain words, so it suits an unfamiliar audience, and everything in it is accurate. However, it reports the study's finding (hellbenders revealed at 14 of 16 sites, five more than hand searches found) rather than the researchers' reason for conducting the study, which is the goal.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. It does state the researchers' reason for conducting the study, but it uses the term "eDNA" without explaining it. The goal is to address readers who do not know what eDNA is, so this sentence would leave them unable to understand what the team tested.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. It explains what the genetic material is, so it suits an unfamiliar audience, but it describes how the team carried out the study (collecting and screening water samples at 16 sites) rather than why the team conducted it, which is the goal.
